hints: Focus on the words 'low concentration of a substrate'. This means neither enzyme is saturated, so do not think about who has the highest top speed.
At very low substrate, success is about affinity (Km), not top speed (Vmax). Recall how a low Vmax enzyme often pairs with a low Km and what that means for grabbing scarce substrate.
walkthrough:
**Spot the key condition: low substrate**

Think of this like two hungry animals competing for very little food. No one is full or working at full speed.

In enzyme terms, both enzymes are working well below their $V_{max}$ because $[S]$ is low.

**Remember what wins when substrate is scarce**

When substrate is scarce, affinity matters more than maximum speed. Affinity is measured by $K_m$: a lower $K_m$ means higher affinity.

$$v = \frac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}$$

At low $[S]$, the enzyme that can grab substrate best will get most of it.

**Link lower Vmax to winning at low substrate**

In this comparison, the enzyme with the lower $V_{max}$ is the specialist for low substrate. It holds substrate tightly and turns it over steadily, so it captures more of the limited substrate molecules.

That is why the enzyme with the lower $V_{max}$ ends up using more of the substrate than the high $V_{max}$ enzyme, which needs lots of substrate to show its power.

options.A: Not correct, the two enzymes will not share equally because they have different kinetic properties and one will outcompete the other at low substrate.
options.B: Not correct, low substrate does not mean no reaction. Both enzymes can still bind substrate and work, just well below Vmax.
options.C: Not correct, this reverses what happens. At low substrate the lower Vmax enzyme is more effective at capturing substrate, so it uses more, not less.
options.D: Correct, at low substrate concentration the enzyme with the lower Vmax outcompetes the other and uses more of the available substrate.
